sections.html:
Woburn is a Middlesex County city about 9 miles north of Boston. It covers roughly 12.9 square miles and shares borders with Wilmington, Reading, Stoneham, Winchester, Lexington and Burlington. The 2020 census counted 40,876 residents in 16,590 households, with 17,540 housing units, about 5.4% of them vacant at the time. A mayor and city council run the city.

Horn Pond, where the town was first settled, is a primary source of the Mystic River. Buyers can compare your house with plenty of others in a city of this size, so price and condition matter more than the address alone.

sections.h2: How much history shows in Woburn houses?
sections.html:
A good deal. Woburn was first settled in 1640 near Horn Pond and became a town in 1642. Its territory once included what are now Winchester, Burlington and parts of Stoneham and Wilmington. The city grew around tanning and transport: a tannery was built in 1668, the Middlesex Canal opened in 1803, and the Boston and Lowell Railroad began running through town in 1835. Route 128 opened in 1951 and Route 93 came through in 1963, which pulled the city toward Boston commuters and offices.

  • Several 18th and 19th century houses survive, including the 1790 House and the Baldwin House beside a stretch of the old canal.
  • The population jumped from about 20,500 in 1950 to 31,200 in 1960 and 37,400 in 1970, so a large share of the housing dates from those postwar decades.

If your house is one of the older ones, a cash buyer prices the age and condition into the offer directly instead of asking you to fix things first.

Woburn is one of the few communities near Boston that supplies its own drinking water. The supply comes mostly from five wells in the Horn Pond aquifer, treated at the Horn Pond Treatment Plant, with about a third supplemented by the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority.

The city also carries a well-known environmental history. High levels of chemical contamination were found in city Wells G and H in 1979, and families in the Pine Street area of east Woburn raised concerns about childhood leukemia. A lawsuit followed in 1982, and the story became the book and film titled A Civil Action.

That history is decades old, but buyers and their lenders sometimes still ask about environmental records on older industrial or neighboring parcels. If your house sits near former industrial land, ask the city's Water Department and the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection what records exist, and share what you learn with any buyer.

sections.h2: Getting around and what it means for value
sections.html:
Woburn sits between two highway corridors, Route 128 and Route 93, with the Anderson Regional Transportation Center as the main transit stop.

  • MBTA Commuter Rail to Boston's North Station and to Lowell.
  • Amtrak service to Portland, Maine.
  • Bus service to Logan International Airport and Manchester-Boston Regional Airport.
  • MBTA bus routes along Main Street, Montvale Avenue, Lexington Street and Cambridge Road.

The older Mishawum commuter rail stop stopped service on December 14, 2020. Distance to the station or the highway ramps is one of the first things a buyer weighs, so mention it when you describe your house.

Woburn Public Schools runs seven elementary schools: Goodyear, Altavesta, Shamrock, Malcolm White, Reeves, Linscott-Rumford and Hurld-Wyman. Students then move to the John F. Kennedy or Daniel L. Joyce middle school and on to Woburn Memorial High School. Northeast Metro Tech serves as the vocational school, and St. Charles is a private Catholic school for kindergarten through eighth grade.

sections.h2: Residential tax rates and holding costs
sections.html:
Property tax is the main carrying cost while you sell, and Woburn publishes its rate history on the Assessing Department page. Rates are per $1,000 of assessed value.

Fiscal yearResidentialCommercial, industrial, personal
2026$9.15$21.43
2025$8.54$20.41
2024$8.06$19.72
2023$8.70$21.14
2022$9.34$22.77

The Assessing Department is on the second floor of City Hall at 10 Common Street, phone 781-897-5830. It handles exemptions for elderly, widowed, blind and disabled veteran owners and posts a homestead page and an abutters list request form. For the rules that apply across the state, see our Massachusetts property tax guide.

A Woburn sale follows Massachusetts law, plus a few local contacts. Three items come up most often.

  • Smoke detectors. Under M.G.L. c. 148, section 26F, the seller must equip a residential building with approved smoke detectors when it is sold or transferred, and the head of the fire department enforces it. Call the Woburn Fire Department to schedule the inspection.
  • Deed excise tax. M.G.L. c. 64D, section 1 sets the excise at $2 for each $500 of consideration, or fraction of it. Your closing attorney will confirm who pays and in what amount.
  • Tax proration. Unpaid or current tax is settled at closing, typically from the seller's proceeds.

These steps are the same whether you list, sell by owner or take a cash offer. What changes is how long they take and how many contingencies surround them. The Registry of Deeds is the one Middlesex County office that stayed in Cambridge, so ask your closing attorney or title company where the deed will be recorded.

sections.h2: How does selling to a cash buyer work in Woburn?
sections.html:
Selling for cash means a buyer purchases the house as it stands, without a mortgage contingency. We look at the address, the condition and any liens or taxes, then present an offer. If you accept, a title company or attorney handles the paperwork and the closing date is set around your timeline.

That path can fit an owner who inherited an older house, who owns a two or three family with a difficult tenant, or who simply does not want to repaint, replace a heating system and hold open houses. You can also turn the offer down and keep your options open.

Before you take any offer, ask for it in writing, check who pays each closing cost and confirm the buyer can show proof of funds. Unpaid or current taxes come out of your proceeds at closing, so ask the Assessing Department for your balance first. A folder with your tax bill, permits and repair receipts speeds every step.

If you are unsure whether to list or sell as is, call or text us and we will walk through both with you, with no pressure to choose.

faqs.q: How far is Woburn from Boston?
faqs.a: Woburn sits about 9 miles north of Boston in Middlesex County. Route 128 and Route 93 both run through the city, and the Anderson Regional Transportation Center offers commuter rail to North Station.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke detector inspection to sell my Woburn house?
faqs.a: Yes. Massachusetts law requires the seller to equip a residential building with approved smoke detectors on sale or transfer, and the head of the fire department enforces it. Contact the Woburn Fire Department to arrange it before closing.

faqs.q: What is the Woburn residential property tax rate?
faqs.a: The city lists $9.15 per $1,000 of assessed value for fiscal year 2026, up from $8.54 in fiscal year 2025. Check the Assessing Department page for the current figure.

faqs.q: Where are deeds recorded for a Woburn sale?
faqs.a: Woburn is in Middlesex County, and the county's Registry of Deeds remained in Cambridge. Your closing attorney or title company records the deed there.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Woburn house that has repairs or tenants?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer purchases as is, so a roof, heating or tenant issue does not have to be solved first. Ask your closing attorney about notice rules if tenants live in the house.
